title: The birds of the air (Matthew 6:25–27)
hookLine: look at the birds: they don't sow or reap, and they're fed

cards: It's two in the morning, and your mind is running the numbers again. Rent. The car.
What if the job goes. What if the test comes back wrong. You lie there doing math that never comes out even.
Now the hillside. Jesus has just said you can't serve God and money, and the obvious question hangs in the air: fine, but then who pays for dinner? He doesn't answer with a budget.
He points up. Look at those birds. They didn't plant anything this morning.

teach.h: TAKE NO THOUGHT: DON'T BE ANXIOUS.
teach.b: In the King James Bible: "Therefore I say unto you, Take no thought for your life, what ye shall eat, or what ye shall drink." Take no thought sounds like don't plan.
But in older English, taking thought could mean being anxious. The Greek word is merimnaō, to worry, to be anxious: half of you in bed, half of you in next month.
Then the picture: "Behold the fowls of the air: for they sow not, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns; yet your heavenly Father feedeth them. Are ye not much better than they?"
The Greek behind behold means look at, look closely. Not glance. Study the bird.
And a careful look shows birds are not lazy. They hunt all day. They build, they fly, they feed their young.
What they don't do is store up barns full of worry. They work without the knot in the stomach.
Then a question that's almost funny: "Which of you by taking thought can add one cubit unto his stature?" A cubit is a measure of length, the forearm. Worry has never made anyone taller.
The Greek can also mean a span of life, so some translations read it as adding an hour to your life. Either way, worry costs a lot and buys nothing. Christians read this in different ways.
Some hear a promise of daily provision; others, an honest reminder that worrying can't change the outcome. Either way, the text doesn't say don't work. The birds are working.

how: Christians often turn to this passage in anxious seasons, reading it slowly or praying the Lord's Prayer line for daily bread, and some make a habit of stepping outside to watch birds as a way of setting worry down.

o: to worry, to be anxious about what's ahead
to trust God completely, without a doubt
to plan carefully and save for the future

games.q: what's inside the passage — tap the pairs.

s: Jesus tells people to stop working like the birds
birds work all day. what they don't do is fill barns with worry.
in older English, take no thought meant don't be anxious
to take thought was to worry. the Greek is merimnaō.
the cubit question may be about length of life, not height
the Greek word can mean stature or a span of life.

games.q: you're on the hillside. Jesus has just said you can't serve God and money. your stomach says: then who pays for dinner? what does he point at?
games.why: "Behold the fowls of the air: for they sow not, neither do they reap." he answers the money question with the birds.

practice: If there's a window near you, watch a bird; if none is in sight, listen for one, or picture the last bird you saw clearly.
Notice how busy it is, and how it doesn't seem to be carrying tomorrow; if a worry shows up, let it sit on the windowsill next to you. If you pray, you can say: give us this day our daily bread.

wordCard.voice: Merimnao, the Greek word for worry, to be anxious. The birds of the air work all day and carry no barns of worry.

orig.note: Greek: to worry, to be anxious; the King James renders it take thought.

carryVoice: Your line: look at the birds. Busy all day, and not carrying tomorrow. Day two hundred fifty-three, done.
